pages.text: Before the sun was up, the zongo was already awake. Traders opened their stalls, a tailor hummed over his sewing machine, and the call to prayer floated over the rooftops. Halima helped her mother fry koose and pour koko for early customers. “Fresh and hot!” she called. The whole street smelled of spice and bean cakes, and she loved it.

“Fresh and hot!” she called.
The whole street smelled of spice and bean cakes, and she loved it.
pages.alt: A girl serves hot food from a stall as the sun rises over rooftops and a mosque.

pages.text: After breakfast, Halima went to Mallam Kadiri’s class for an hour of Arabic and the Quran. She sat among children of all ages, all reciting together. “Learning is a treasure,” said Mallam Kadiri. “It cannot be stolen, and it grows when you share it.” Then Halima hurried home, changed into her school uniform and set off for the junior high school, a short walk away.

pages.alt: Children sit on mats reciting with a teacher in a white kaftan before school.

pages.text: At school, Halima was the best in English. But during break, a boy from another class sneered, “You people from the zongo only trade and fight.” Halima’s throat tightened. Then she remembered her street: the tailor who made school uniforms for free, the traders who paid fees for orphans, the imam who settled quarrels. “That is not true,” she said calmly. “Come and see.”
sentences: At school, Halima was the best in English.
But during break, a boy from another class sneered, “You people from the zongo only trade and fight.” Halima’s throat tightened.
Then she remembered her street: the tailor who made school uniforms for free, the traders who paid fees for orphans, the imam who settled quarrels.
“That is not true,” she said calmly.
“Come and see.”
pages.alt: A girl faces a boy on a school field, standing tall while others watch.

pages.text: Mr Obeng had heard. After class, he asked Halima to tell the whole class about her community. She was nervous, but she began: “The word zongo is often said to come from a Hausa word for a place where travellers rest. Many of us come from different places, languages and traditions, but we share one street.” The class listened. Mr Obeng nodded. “Every community has strengths and struggles,” he said. “Judging by one is not fair.”

pages.text: But life was not easy. That evening, Halima’s father sat quietly with a notebook of bills. School fees were due, and the stall had earned less that week. Halima offered to stop school. “Never,” said her father. “Your education is our greatest investment.” Her aunt Latifa joined the family. “The neighbourhood association will help with part of it,” she said. “That is what neighbours are for.”

“The neighbourhood association will help with part of it,” she said.
“That is what neighbours are for.”
pages.alt: A family sits around a lamp with a notebook of bills while an aunt offers help.

pages.text: On Friday evening, after prayers, the whole zongo gathered at the field. Wahab and his friends played football against a team from another neighbourhood. Halima cheered from the edge. The match ended in a draw, and both teams shook hands and shared water. “That is the zongo,” said her aunt, smiling. “Hard work, faith and good sport.”

pages.text: That night, Halima wrote a narrative paragraph for English homework. “It was a Friday evening in the zongo, and the setting sun painted the rooftops gold. Boys chased a battered ball across the dusty field while their families cheered. When the final whistle blew, the two teams shook hands and laughed together. I felt proud to belong to a place where kindness is never in short supply.”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: a narrative paragraph uses past tense throughout, strong verbs such as “chased” and “painted”, and a sense of time and place. Halima began with “It was a Friday evening” and ended with a feeling. Notice that she wrote “was” and “chased”, never “is” and “chase” in the same paragraph. Keep the tense steady. The end.
